title: Beyond words
hookLine: Moses runs after the shepherd, who has gone past speech altogether (Masnavi 2)

cards: Running after someone to apologize goes like this. Out the door, down the street, heart going, rehearsing the words. And sometimes, on catching up, it turns out they've already moved on.
Not in anger. They've just gone somewhere that can't quite be followed anymore. Moses has been rebuked.
He knows he has to find the shepherd and set things right. So the prophet goes out into the desert, running. Today, the last part of the story.

teach.b: Moses follows the shepherd's footprints in the sand, and they're all over the place: the steps of someone lost in his own heart, one like a castle on a chessboard, going straight, another like a bishop, going slantwise.
Finally Moses catches up, with good news.
You have permission, he says. Don't look for rules or proper forms. Say whatever your heart wants to say.
Your way of praying is the light of faith. It sounds like the happy ending. It isn't.
The shepherd answers: Moses, I've gone past that now. I'm soaked in my heart's blood.

In Rumi's telling he has passed beyond the Lote Tree, the tree that in Islamic tradition marks the farthest boundary of heaven. You struck my horse with your whip, he tells Moses, and it leapt and went beyond the sky.
And then: my state now is beyond telling. What I'm saying to you isn't my state. The scolding didn't just hurt him.
It pushed him past the need for words altogether. Then Rumi turns to the reader. Whatever you say in praise of God, he says, is like the image a mirror shows.
The picture is yours, not the mirror's. On Rumi's reading, words about the sacred are never the sacred itself. Even the proper ones.
Even Moses's. Yesterday was about not judging someone's words. Today goes one step further: at the deepest point, maybe no words fit.
Your line: soaked in my heart's blood.

how: Many traditions keep a practice of silent prayer or contemplation alongside spoken prayer, and some of Rumi's lyric poems close on the word for silent.

o: past the point where speech can say it
a prayer said silently in your head
something too secret to tell anyone

games.q: what goes with what — tap the pairs.
p: the picture is yours, not the mirror's

s: the shepherd is overjoyed and goes back to his old prayer
he says he's gone past that. his state is now beyond telling.
Moses tells him to say whatever his heart wants
he brings permission: no rules, no proper forms.
Rumi says our praise of God is like an image in a mirror
the picture is ours, not the mirror's. words about the sacred aren't the sacred.

games.q: you're the shepherd. Moses has run across the desert to tell you that you can pray any way you like. what do you say?
o: thank you; I'll go back to combing God's hair.
I'm still angry; leave me alone.
I've gone past that now; my state is beyond telling.
games.why: the shepherd says the scolding sent him beyond the sky, and that what he says is no longer his state.

practice: Let the words in your head slow down, the way traffic thins late at night; when a sentence starts, you don't have to finish it, just let it trail off. Rest in whatever is there before the words.
If you pray, this can be a prayer with nothing said.

wordCard.voice: Beyond words. Moses runs after the shepherd to give him permission to pray his own way, and finds he has gone past speech altogether. Today's word.

orig.note: Persian: silent, hushed. some of Rumi's lyric poems close on this word.

carryVoice: Your line: soaked in my heart's blood. Some things are bigger than words. That's day one hundred ninety-six.

sources.work: The Qur'an (the Lote Tree of the utmost boundary, described)
